title: People With This Neanderthal Hormone Receptor Have More Muscle Mass
gist: A Current Biology study finds the Neanderthal growth hormone receptor variant makes cultured muscle cells respond more strongly to human growth hormone and grow 40 percent larger than normal cells; the variant entered modern humans via interbreeding roughly 47,000 years ago and is carried by about 24 percent of South Asians versus around 0.5 percent of Europeans.

themes.theme: A single receptor variant with a large effect

insights.claim: Muscle cells cultured to express the Neanderthal growth hormone receptor responded more strongly to human growth hormone and grew 40 percent larger than normal cells — a functional effect demonstrated in vitro, not merely inferred from genetics.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A 40 percent in vitro response gap on a known druggable axis makes this receptor variant an obvious target for muscle-wasting and metabolic research.
insights.quote: When they cultured muscle cells expressing the Neanderthal receptor, they responded more strongly to human growth hormone, growing 40 percent larger than normal cells.

insights.claim: The Neanderthal growth hormone receptor differs from the modern human version by only slight alterations, meaning a small sequence change is enough to shift hormone sensitivity substantially.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Small-edit, large-effect receptor variants are the highest-leverage targets for engineered therapeutics.

insights.claim: The variant entered modern humans through interbreeding with Neanderthals around 47,000 years ago and is now roughly 48 times more common in South Asians (about 24 percent) than in Europeans (around 0.5 percent).
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Extreme frequency skew across populations means any study or trial recruiting only European-ancestry cohorts would have almost entirely missed this variant.
insights.quote: Today, it’s fairly common in populations in South and East Asia, present in roughly 24 percent of South Asians (compared with around 0.5 percent of Europeans).

insights.claim: Neanderthals were shorter and stockier but more muscular than Homo sapiens, and this receptor difference is offered as a mechanistic explanation for that long-observed morphological gap.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Converting a descriptive fossil observation into a molecular mechanism is what makes archaic-genome work translatable rather than purely historical.
